DeSurv allows patient survival to shape gene-program discovery, yielding a tumor--stroma architecture that connects prognostic information with interpretable malignant and stromal programs. In PDAC, the architecture comprised a dominant survival-aligned program, D1, characterized by coordinated cross-patient variation in classical tumor and restCAF-like stromal features, alongside separately resolved proCAF-like stromal and basal-like tumor programs. D1 remained prognostic after adjustment for the established PurIST and DeCAF classifications. The frozen programs transferred without refitting to four independent external cohorts.

An unsupervised control at $\alpha = 0$, matched to DeSurv on rank and tuning budget, did not recover D1, so the difference in the recovered programs did not appear to reflect rank or tuning effort. A rank-optimized unsupervised control recovered comparable prognostic information across a broader seven-factor representation, and conventional supervised predictors achieved similar discrimination while combining contributions from underlying expression programs within single scores. These comparisons separate prognostic information from the representation in which it is recovered. DeSurv retains the contributing sources as separately scored programs rather than combining them within a composite predictor.

This distinction clarifies the role of the frozen gene-program basis. In DeSurv, survival acts directly on the gene-program matrix $W$ while the reconstruction objective requires the learned programs to continue representing the observed transcriptome. Once learned, the gene weights are held fixed, so external validation tests the same programs rather than a newly estimated representation. In CoxNMF and SurvNMF, the survival term depends on sample-side latent representations [@huang2020low; @le2025survnmf]. In DeSurv, it depends directly on projections through the gene-program matrix, and new samples are scored with fixed gene weights without a sample-loading estimation step (Supplementary Table \ref{tab:architecture}). Deep latent-variable survival models [@zaccaria2023surviae; @meng2022savae] likewise learn sample representations rather than a fixed gene-program basis, and reference-based deconvolution methods such as CIBERSORTx [@newman2019cibersortx] and BayesPrism [@chu2022bayesprism] estimate the abundance of predefined cell types rather than outcome-aligned programs and are complementary to DeSurv.

Program-level outputs are the practical product of this architecture, because the genes defining each program determine its interpretation and what can be tested next. Previous PDAC studies illustrate how interpretable malignant and stromal programs can support biological characterization and single-sample classifiers [@moffitt2015virtual; @peng2019novo; @rashid2020purity; @peng2024determination]. DeSurv extends this line of work by allowing patient outcomes to influence the gene weights themselves while retaining separately measurable programs: for example, D2 remains available as proCAF-like stromal context although the fitted risk score combines D1 and D3. Where molecular annotations are lacking, the ranked genes defining each program could seed biological annotation, subtype development and reduced biomarker assays. These outputs do not yet establish clinical utility or a treatment-selection rule.

Rank choice and initialization can affect the recovered gene programs. Increasing rank progressively broadened correspondence to established PDAC programs. The three-factor DeSurv solution and the seven-factor unsupervised control were selected by the same one-standard-error rule. Survival supervision provides an outcome-informed criterion for shaping the representation but does not remove the non-uniqueness of matrix factorization, and individual runs from different random starts recover appreciably different gene sets. Split-half consensus fits agreed closely with the reported basis (Supplementary Information, Stability of the recovered gene programs), supporting stability to restart-pool composition within the training data but not establishing reproducibility under independent repetition or patient resampling.

The simulations identify conditions under which survival information improves program recovery. They provide a controlled example in which survival supervision prioritizes prognostically relevant programs that contribute little expression variation and are therefore less readily recovered by reconstruction-driven factorization.

Three statistical qualifications limit interpretation of the prognostic findings. DeSurv uses a proportional-hazards objective, while the external validation data showed attenuation of the prognostic association over follow-up (Schoenfeld test, Results), so the reported hazard ratios are time-averaged summaries and extensions could accommodate non-proportional or nonlinear hazards. The integrated Brier analysis recalibrated the score's scalar slope and baseline hazard within each validation dataset, so it describes apparent prediction error rather than out-of-sample error (Supplementary Information, Proper-scoring sensitivity of the external validation). The pooled training objective was fitted without a cohort term; within-cohort analyses argued against simple encoding of training-cohort membership, although cohort influence on the learned representation remains possible (Supplementary Information, Cohort handling in the training objective).

In treated cohorts the frozen scores remained informative in exploratory analyses, but arm-level sample sizes limited assessment of variation across treatments. Whether these programs predict differential treatment benefit therefore remains unresolved and will require adequately powered, prespecified treatment-by-program interaction analyses.

The tumor--stroma architecture described here is a bulk-tissue phenomenon. It reflects cross-patient covariation in tumor- and stroma-associated transcriptional programs rather than cellular co-expression or spatial adjacency within individual tumors. This is consistent with broader evidence that malignant lineage state and stromal composition vary together in PDAC [@ogawa2020stroma; @neuzillet2022periostin; @lee2024tumorcaf]. Purity adjustment in the PACA-AU datasets left the risk score's association essentially unchanged. GATA6 RNA in situ hybridization independently supports D1's classical tumor component; these analyses do not establish the cellular identity of its stromal component. Single-cell or spatial profiling could clarify the cellular sources of these programs, but linking those sources to prognosis would require outcome-annotated cohorts and platform-appropriate scoring.

The question DeSurv addresses extends beyond PDAC. In any tumor type, the programs that dominate expression variation may differ from those most relevant to survival, so outcome information could help prioritize programs that reconstruction alone underweights. Testing generalizability will require multi-cancer evaluation of prognostic performance, program recovery and stability, with attention to cohort composition and event counts. Comparators should include unsupervised decompositions and strong penalized-regression baselines, which remain difficult to outperform consistently for out-of-sample prognosis [@smith2020standard].

In PDAC, incorporating survival during factorization recovered a three-program tumor--stroma architecture that transferred across independent cohorts while retaining biological components that could be interrogated separately. More generally, DeSurv provides a framework for asking not only whether transcriptomic data predict outcome, but which biological programs are recovered when outcome information helps shape their discovery.
